why: The four `require` shapes the front-end reads — whole module (a namespace), destructured, `.member`, and a package — each through its own callee, so a break in any one cannot hide behind another. Plus the one it deliberately does not bind: a renamed destructuring, where resolution would name the target by the local. `format.js` exports a real `cash` as a decoy, so a binding by the local name would land on a real node and trip the refusal — without the decoy, `finalize` dropped the wrong edge anyway and the refusal could never fire.

known_gaps.why: PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING. `const { money: cash } = require('./format')` binds `cash` to the export `money`, but resolution names an imported callee by its *local* name, so binding it would send `cash()` to `ts:lib/format.cash`. The front-end records the import and binds nothing. A true edge, counted as a recall miss.

refusals.why: PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING. What a reader that binds renamed destructurings by the local name would emit. `format.js` really exports a `cash` — the decoy — so the wrong edge would land on a real node and neither the export map nor the existence check could stop it: only the binding rule does.

excluded: `exports.pad = pad` adds no node: the value is an identifier, and `pad` is already declared under the id a caller's `format.pad()` resolves to.
